clips.title: What is RPC? gRPC Introduction.
clips.why: A clear picture of what a remote procedure call is and how protocol buffers turn messages into bytes, which is the wire our fake sits behind.
look: A remote call looks like a local function call, but the arguments travel as bytes.
Protocol buffers: a .proto file describes each message, and code is generated from it.
Client stub on one side, server on the other: our fake is the server side.
clips.after: The cloud talks to every on-prem client this way, through one proxy call that carries the method name and the request bytes.

clips.title: Python gRPC Tutorial - Create a gRPC Client and Server in Python with Various Types of gRPC Calls
clips.why: Shows how a Python gRPC server is built from the generated servicer class, the same three steps our fixture does.
look: The server class subclasses the generated servicer and implements its methods.
add_..._to_server registers it, and the server listens on a port.
The methods take a request message and return a response message, never a dict.
clips.after: FakeAgents is such a servicer; the fixture starts it on port 0 inside the test and the cloud's real client calls it.

clips.title: Unit Tests and Test Doubles like Mocks, Stubs & Fakes
clips.why: Names the kinds of test doubles, so you can say precisely why a fake is different from a mock.
look: A test double is anything that stands in for a real dependency in a test.
The difference between a double that only answers and one that really works.
Where each kind fits, and what each one cannot tell you.
clips.after: fcp's cloud tests mostly use mocks at this boundary; the new API layer uses fakes with contract suites instead.

practice.q: Which test would have caught the TypeError from the story before it shipped?

options.text: A mock that returns {"is_healthy": True, "version": 2}, with more fields.
options.why: More fields in the made-up answer do not change its type. It is still a dict, and the real client never returns one.

options.text: A test that calls site_status with the real client talking to a fake gRPC server.
options.why: The real client decodes real bytes into a HealthCheckResponse, so the code meets the real type and fails like production.

options.text: A test that asserts the mock was called once with "HealthCheck".
options.why: That checks how the code calls the client, not what it does with the answer. It passes with the bug.

practice.q: The fixture starts the fake server. Fill in the port that lets the operating system choose a free one.
practice.why: Port 0 asks the operating system for any free port, and add_insecure_port returns the one it got, so tests never collide.

practice.q: Where does the fixture point the real client? Fill in the call that changes the address only for this test.
practice.hint: monkeypatch has a method for environment variables.
practice.why: The real client reads the address each time it is created, so changing it at the seam is enough and is undone after the test.

practice.q: Put one call from site_status to the fake in order.
items: site_status creates the real AgentClient, which reads the proxy address
The client encodes HealthCheckRequest into bytes and calls AgentRpc with the method name
The fake looks the method up, decodes the bytes with the real request type and runs its handler
The fake encodes a HealthCheckResponse into bytes and returns it
The client decodes the bytes into a HealthCheckResponse, and site_status reads is_healthy
practice.why: Everything except the handler is production code or real gRPC, which is why the fake catches type and encoding mistakes.

practice.q: The real proxy answers an offline client with error type TIMEOUT. What should the fake do for an agent in offline?

options.why: AgentOffline belongs to the cloud's client. If the fake raised it, the client's own handling of TIMEOUT would never be tested.

options.text: Answer with error type TIMEOUT, like the real proxy.
options.why: Then the real client turns it into AgentOffline, exactly as in production, and site_status shows offline.

options.text: Wait forever, so the call times out for real.
options.why: That would make tests slow and still not match what the proxy answers.

practice.q: A contract test passes with --target fake and fails with --target lab. What does that tell you?

options.text: The Lab is flaky; rerun it until it passes.
options.why: Maybe, but a contract test exists to catch exactly this difference. Read the failure first.

options.text: The fake no longer behaves like the real client for this case, so fix the fake (or the contract) before trusting tests that use it.
options.why: That difference is drift, and the contract suite is the place where it becomes visible.

options.text: The contract test is wrong and should be deleted.
options.why: Deleting it hides the drift. Tests that use the fake would keep trusting a wrong answer.
